structure.title: **I. Introduction**
structure.text:
A lithium battery has an advantage of obtaining a high energy density because of its high electrochemical potential and light weight. A high Li + conducting solid electrolyte at room temperature has been investigated as the application for an all solid state lithium battery.

Goodenough et al. [1,2] discovered a Na + super ionic conductor of *Na~+xZrzP3\_xSixO~2* (NASI-CON). LiME(PO4)3, M=Ge [3,4], Ti [5-15], Sn, Hf [ 15,16 ], Zr [ 16,17 ] also possess the NASICONtype structure. We have already reported that LiTi2(PO4)3 has the most suitable lattice size (cell volume ca. 1309/~3, space group R3c) for Li + migration in the NASICON-type Li + conductors [ 15 ]. A minimum activation energy of 0.28-0.30 eV for a bulk component was obtained for the Li + conductors based on LiTi2 (PO4) 3. In this paper, the electrical properties and the crystal structure were examined for the NASICON-type solid electrolytes based on LiHf2(PO4)3, i.e. LiHf2(PO4)3+yLi20 system and Li~+xMxHf2\_x- (PO4)3 (M=Cr, Fe, Sc, In, Lu or Y) system.

We have reported that the conductivity at around room temperature is mainly controlled by that of grain boundaries for these NASICON-type ceramic electrolytes [15]. structure.title: *2. I. Materials*
structure.text: LizCO 3 (purity: 99.99%), HfO2 (99.9%), (NH4) 2HPO4 ( extra pure grade ), and M203 M = Cr, Fe, Sc, In, Lu, or Y (99.9% or 99.99%) were used as starting materials. The mixture was reacted in a platinum crucible at 1173 K for two hours in air. The starting materials of Li2CO 3 and (NH4)2HPO4 decomposed into Li20 and P205 by the heat treatment. The resulting material was ground into a fine powder using a ball-mill for six hours (wet process: methanol). The dried powder was again reacted at 1173 K for two hours in air and then reground by the same ball-milling method. The particle size of the powder was smaller than 1 ~tm. Dried powder mixed with a suitable amount of 3 wt% PVA solution was pressed into a pellet at a pressure of 1 × 108 Pa. The pellet was sintered for two hours in air. Gold electrodes were sputtered on both polished surfaces of the electrolyte by an Ion Coater (Shimadzu IC-50).

structure.text:
The relationship between the sintering temperature and the porosity of the sintered pellet is shown in fig. 2. The high density pellet could not be obtained for LiHf2(PO4)3 even if the sintering temperature raised to 1593 K. On the other hand, high density pellet can be obtained for the samples with Li20 addition. Li20 acts as a flux to form a high density sample. The effect of the Li20 addition has been already reported in our previous papers [15 ]. The porosity greatly decreased by the sintering at around 1173 K, and then increased by the elevation of the sintered temperature for all the Li20 added samples. Fig. 3 shows the surface microstructure of the sintered LiHf2 (PO4) 3 + 0.3Li20 samples. The grains are closely contacted with one another for the sample heated at 1173 K (fig. 3a). The particle size was smaller than 1 ~tm, which is almost the same as that ![](_page_2_Figure_2.jpeg) Fig. 2. Relationship between the porosity and the sintered temperature for LiHf2(PO4)a+yLi20 system: y=0 (O); 0.1 (•); 0.2 (V);0.3 (11); 0.4 (0). of the ball-milled powder. The surface of the sintered sample is very smooth. No other peaks without those of LiHf2(PO4)3 can be detected from the X-ray diffraction patterns for all LiHf2(PO4)3+yLi20 system. In addition, the lithium atom did not evaporate by the heating process, which was confirmed by an atomic absorption measurement. The added Li20 would exist as a glassy phase at grain boundaries. However, Li20 itself has a high melting point. We presume that the glassy lithium phosphate would be formed at elevated temperature from the added Li20 and phosphate. The grain size grew with the elevation of the sintering temperature (b). The fine granules appeared on LiHfz (PO4) 3 grains. The granules would be the lithium phosphate or Li20 which acts as a flux. Some pores observed between the particles appeared in fig. 3b. The increase in the pellet porosity with the sintering temperature (in fig. 2 ) might result from the fact that the pore size at the grain boundary increased with the particle growth. The particle growth greatly accelerated for the sample sintered at 1393 K (fig. 3c). In this case, cracks are observed in the grains. Fig. 4 presents the temperature dependence of the total (bulk plus grain boundary component) conductivity for LiHf2(PO4)3+0.3Li20 sample. The conductivity greatly enhanced for the samples sintered at above 1293 K. The D-Fe2(SO4)3-type (P21/ n) monoclinic phase was formed for the samples sintered at temperature lower than 1293 K. The slope of the aT- 1/T relation decreased by the formation of the NASICON-type structure. It seems that the Li + ion does not easily migrate in the monoclinic phase. Fig. 5 shows the relationship between the activation energy for the total conductivity and the sintering temperature. The activation energy was determined in the temperature range from room temperature to 400 K. The activation energy abruptly decreased with the sintering temperature for all the samples. The decrease in the activation energies is attributed to the P2~/n--. R3c phase transition. Although the samples calcined at 1173 K during the preparation process, R3c phase could not be formed for all the calcined powder. The obtained rhombohedral phase did not revert to the monoclinic phase by cooling. The phase transition temperature is about 1423 K for LiH%(PO4)3 y=0, and the temperature decreased with the Li20 addition. The transition temperature for Li20 added samples is close to that of the high densification (in fig. 2). The decrease of the transition temperature might be influenced by the high sinterability. Fig. 6 shows the total conductivity at 298 K for LiTi2 (PO4) 3 +yLi20 system, the conductivity considerably increased with the sintering temperature. It is considered that the conductivity was enhanced by both the formation of the NASICONtype phase and the decrease in the porosity. Although the porosity decreased for the monoclinic samples of y=0.3 and 0.4 sintered at 1173 K, the conductivity enhancement with high densification is smaller than that with the formation of NASICONtype phase. The conductivity enhancement mainly occurred by the formation of the NASICON-type phase. The conductivity also greatly enhanced by the Li20 addition. For Li20 added samples, a maximum conductivity was obtained for the samples sintered at ca. 1298 K. The conductivity decreased for the samples sintered above 1298 K. The particle growth might affect the decrease of the conductivity (see fig. 3). The maximum conductivity is 1.1 × 10 -4 S.cm-1 for LiHf2(PO4)3+0.1Li20 sintered at 1298 K. nodes.text: Fig. 5 shows the relationship between the activation energy for the total conductivity and the sintering temperature. The activation energy was determined in the temperature range from room temperature to 400 K. The activation energy abruptly decreased with the sintering temperature for all the samples. The decrease in the activation energies is attributed to the P2~/n--. R3c phase transition. Although the samples calcined at 1173 K during the preparation process, R3c phase could not be formed for all the calcined powder. The obtained rhombohedral phase did not revert to the monoclinic phase by cooling. The phase transition temperature is about 1423 K for LiH%(PO4)3 y=0, and the temperature decreased with the Li20 addition. The transition temperature for Li20 added samples is close to that of the high densification (in fig. 2). The decrease of the transition temperature might be influenced by the high sinterability.

nodes.text:
Fig. 6 shows the total conductivity at 298 K for LiTi2 (PO4) 3 +yLi20 system, the conductivity considerably increased with the sintering temperature. It is considered that the conductivity was enhanced by both the formation of the NASICONtype phase and the decrease in the porosity. Although the porosity decreased for the monoclinic samples of y=0.3 and 0.4 sintered at 1173 K, the conductivity enhancement with high densification is smaller than that with the formation of NASICONtype phase. The conductivity enhancement mainly occurred by the formation of the NASICON-type phase. The conductivity also greatly enhanced by the Li20 addition. For Li20 added samples, a maximum conductivity was obtained for the samples sintered at ca. 1298 K. The conductivity decreased for the samples sintered above 1298 K. The particle growth might affect the decrease of the conductivity (see fig. 3). The maximum conductivity is 1.1 × 10 -4 S.cm-1 for LiHf2(PO4)3+0.1Li20 sintered at 1298 K.

nodes.title: Bulk and Grain Boundary Conductivity and Activation Energy
nodes.text:
The conductivities for the bulk and the grain boundary were determined from these results. Table 1 shows the activation energy for  $\operatorname{Li^+}$  conduction of the bulk and the grain boundary for  $\operatorname{LiHf_2(PO_4)_3} + y \operatorname{Li_2O}$  (rhombohedral sample). nodes.title: Summary of Findings and Application Prospects
nodes.text: In conclusion, the electrical properties were studied for the ceramic electrolytes based on LiHf2 (PO4) 3. The phase transition from P2 t/n phase to NASICON-type R3c structure was observed at above 1173 K. The conductivity was greatly enhanced by the addition of the lithium compound and partial substitution of HP ÷ site by M 3+ ion because of the high densification and the decrease in the activation energy at the grain boundary. The M 3+ substitution did not affect the activation energy for bulk component. The activation energy for bulk component is 0.42 eV for LiHf2 (PO4)3 system, and is higher than 0.30 eV of LiTi2(PO4)3 system. The tunnel size for a Li ÷ migration of LiHf2 (PO4)3 system is larger than a suitable size. The maximum conductivity of 1.7× 10 -4 S.cm -1 at 298 K was obtained for presented LiHf2 (PO4) 3 systems, and the value is smaller than 7.0× 10 -4 S.cm -1 [ 10,11 ] of LiTi2(PO4)'3 systems. However, the Hf-system is superior for the application such as battery and gas sensors, since the tetravalent HP + cation is more stable toward a lithium metal and reductive gases than Ti 4÷ ion.
